a: Strike him down!" And they struck him in his chariot on the climb to Gur
p: The Hebrew lacks "and they struck him": Jehu's order runs straight into the place name. The ancient versions supply it.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate ("et percusserunt eum"); with a singular verb, the Septuagint ("and he struck him"); most modern translations
readings.orig: et percusserunt eum (Latin, plural; = וַיַּכֻּהוּ); καὶ ἐπάταξεν αὐτόν (Greek, singular; = וַיַּכֵּהוּ)
readings.en: Strike him! And they (Greek: he) struck him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur
readings.plain: Strike him down!" And they struck him in his chariot on the climb to Gur

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV supplies "And they did so"
readings.en: Strike him (into) the chariot, at the ascent of Gur
readings.plain: Strike him down in his chariot!" This was on the climb to Gur

why: The Hebrew reads awkwardly: an order is followed at once by a place, with no report that it was carried out, and then "he fled." A verb, wayyakkuhu, "and they struck him," looks very like the hakkuhu, "strike him," just before it, so a copyist's eye could easily skip from one to the other. The Greek and the Latin both have a verb, though the Greek (Vaticanus, as printed by Rahlfs) makes it singular, "he struck him," meaning Jehu, and the Latin plural. The Plain therefore follows the versions; the meaning hardly changes, since the next words assume Ahaziah was wounded.

p: The Hebrew says "he trampled her," meaning Jehu. The ancient versions have "they trampled her," the horses or the men.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV ("he trode her under foot")
Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate; RSV, ESV

why: The singular verb is the harder reading and makes Jehu himself drive his chariot over the queen, which fits the brutal scene. The plural may be a translator's smoothing after "the horses." The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

t: Officials of Jezreel, or of the city?
p: Why would Jezreel's officials be in Samaria? The Greek and Latin name the officials of Samaria or of "the city."

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV
Lucianic Greek manuscripts, as reported (the better witness to the Old Greek in this kaige section); Latin Vulgate ("ad optimates civitatis")
readings.orig: πρὸς τοὺς ἄρχοντας τῆς πόλεως (= אֶל־שָׂרֵי הָעִיר)
readings.en: to the officials of the city

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (as printed by Rahlfs)
readings.orig: πρὸς τοὺς ἄρχοντας Σαμαρείας (= אֶל־שָׂרֵי שֹׁמְרוֹן)

why: The letters are sent to Samaria, so "officials of the city" (Samaria) reads more smoothly, and 10:5–6 speaks of "the man over the city" and "the great men of the city." But the Hebrew is the harder reading and can be explained: Jezreel was the royal winter residence, and its officials may have fled to the capital, or the court of Jezreel may have been in Samaria with the princes. Codex Vaticanus, usually revised toward the Hebrew in this part of Kings, here reads "the officials of Samaria," which looks like another attempt to smooth the same difficulty. The Lucianic reading is reported from the editions and commentaries; it was not checked in a manuscript. The Plain keeps the Hebrew; many scholars prefer "the city."

t: Guardians of Ahab, or of Ahab's sons?
p: The Hebrew says "the guardians, Ahab," with no word for "sons." The Greek has "of the sons of Ahab."

readings.w: Septuagint (Vaticanus, as printed by Rahlfs); most modern translations
readings.orig: πρὸς τοὺς τιθηνοὺς υἱῶν Αχααβ (= הָאֹמְנֵי בְנֵי אַחְאָב)
readings.en: to the guardians of the sons of Ahab

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Latin Vulgate ("ad nutricios Ahab"); KJV "them that brought up Ahab's children" (with "children" in italics)

why: The Hebrew "the guardians, Ahab" is hard to construe; it probably means "Ahab's guardians," the men raising his sons, as 10:5 ("those bringing up the sons") and 10:6 show. The Greek supplies "sons," which may be a translator's help or may preserve a word lost from the Hebrew. The Plain follows the Greek here, since the sense is not in doubt and English needs the word.

a: the standing stones out of the house of Baal and burned it
p: The Hebrew has plural "standing stones" but "burned it." The Greek and Latin have one pillar, which they burn.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV "images ... burned them"
readings.en: they brought out the pillars of the house of Baal and burned it
readings.plain: the standing stones out of the house of Baal and burned it

readings.w: Septuagint (Vaticanus, as printed by Rahlfs) and Latin Vulgate ("statuam")
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξήνεγκαν τὴν στήλην τοῦ Βααλ καὶ ἐνέπρησαν αὐτήν (= מַצֶּבֶת)
readings.en: they brought out the pillar of Baal and burned it
readings.plain: the standing stone out of the house of Baal and burned it

why: The Hebrew has the plural here and the singular in 10:27 ("Baal's standing stone"); the Greek has them the other way round (one pillar in 10:26, "pillars" in 10:27). Both texts show that copyists or translators struggled with stones that are burned. Many scholars read asherah, a wooden pole, in 10:26. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, including the singular "it," and the note on this verse discusses the problem.

a: him and his nurse, into the room where the beds were kept. They hid him
p: Kings says "they hid him," with no verb for putting him in the room. Chronicles and the Greek say "she hid him."

readings.w: Masoretic Text of 2 Kings; KJV
readings.orig: אֹתוֹ וְאֶת־מֵינִקְתּוֹ בַּחֲדַר הַמִּטּוֹת וַיַּסְתִּרוּ אֹתוֹ
readings.en: him and his nurse in the room of the beds. And they hid him
readings.plain: him and his nurse, into the room where the beds were kept. They hid him

readings.w: 2 Chronicles 22:11 ("she put him and his nurse ... she hid him"); Septuagint of Kings (Vaticanus, "and she hid him")
readings.orig: וַתִּתֵּן אֹתוֹ וְאֶת־מֵינִקְתּוֹ בַּחֲדַר הַמִּטּוֹת ... וַתַּסְתִּירֵהוּ
readings.en: she put him and his nurse in the room of the beds ... and she hid him
readings.plain: him and his nurse, and she put them in the room where the beds were kept. She hid him

why: The Hebrew of Kings is short: "him and his nurse" hangs without a verb, and the plural "they hid" brings in the nurse or others as helpers. Chronicles supplies "she put" and makes Jehosheba hide him alone; the Greek of Kings has "she hid him" but no added verb. The Plain keeps the plural of Kings and lets "him and his nurse" follow "stole him out."

p: The first killer's name is Jozabad in the Leningrad Codex but Jozacar in the printed Hebrew tradition and the ancient versions.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex as transcribed in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (and this site's word list); compare 2 Chronicles 24:26 "Zabad"; NIV, BSB
BHS as printed and the older printed Hebrew Bibles, as reported; Septuagint (Vaticanus, "Iezichar"), Latin Vulgate ("Iosachar"), Syriac as reported; KJV "Jozachar", ESV and NASB "Jozacar"

why: The two names differ by one letter, b (ב) and k (כ), which look alike. The Westminster transcription of the Leningrad Codex, the base text here, reads Jozabad, and Chronicles' short form "Zabad" (2 Chronicles 24:26) agrees. The printed tradition behind the KJV and ESV, and the Greek and Latin, have the k form, so Jozacar is old and well supported. Printed editions are reported to differ on what the Leningrad Codex itself shows here; that could not be checked in a facsimile. The Plain keeps Jozabad with the Leningrad transcription. On Chronicles' different account of the killers, see the note on 12:20.

a: Hazael king of Aram had crushed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.
t: A Greek addition about the Philistines
p: The Greek adds that Hazael took Philistia from Jehoahaz's control, from the western sea to Aphek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV and most translations
readings.orig: וַחֲזָאֵל מֶלֶךְ אֲרָם לָחַץ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל כֹּל יְמֵי יְהוֹאָחָז
readings.en: Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.
readings.plain: Hazael king of Aram had crushed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.

readings.w: Lucianic Greek manuscripts, as reported (not in Codex Vaticanus as printed by Rahlfs)
readings.orig: καὶ ἔλαβεν Αζαηλ τὸν ἀλλόφυλον ἐκ χειρὸς αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ θαλάσσης τῆς καθ᾽ ἑσπέραν ἕως Αφεκ
readings.en: ... and Hazael took the Philistine from his hand, from the western sea to Aphek.
readings.plain: Hazael king of Aram had crushed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. Hazael took the Philistines out of his hand, from the western sea as far as Aphek.

why: The addition fits Hazael's campaign against Gath (12:17) and the mention of Aphek in Elisha's prophecy (13:17). Some scholars think it preserves an old note dropped from the Hebrew; others think a Greek editor composed it from 12:17. Because the Hebrew is shorter and the addition may be a learned expansion, the Plain follows the Hebrew. Codex Vaticanus, revised toward the Hebrew in this section, does not have the addition; it is a Lucianic reading, and the Lucianic text is the better witness to the Old Greek here. It is reported from the editions and commentaries and was not checked in a manuscript.

p: The written Hebrew spells the queen mother's name Jehoaddin; the reading tradition and Chronicles have Jehoaddan.

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); 2 Chronicles 25:1; KJV
Masoretic written text (Ketiv)

why: Only one vowel letter differs. The Masoretes marked the written form to be read as in Chronicles, and the Plain follows the reading tradition, as most translations do. The name means "the LORD is delight."

p: The Hebrew "before the people" uses an odd, Aramaic-looking word. The Lucianic Greek reads "at Ibleam."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (qabal-'am); KJV, NIV
Lucianic Greek manuscripts (ἐν Ιεβλααμ), as reported, the better witness to the Old Greek here; RSV, ESV
Codex Vaticanus (as printed by Rahlfs), which reads the letters as a name

why: Qabal, "in front of" (Aramaic qŏbēl), is an Aramaic word found in Daniel and Ezra but nowhere else in pre-exilic Hebrew, which makes many scholars suspect a copying error for beyivle'am, "at Ibleam." Ibleam is where Jehu's men struck Ahaziah (9:27), so the Lucianic reading would have the last king of Jehu's line die where Jehu's purge began (9:27). Vaticanus treats the same letters as a man's name, Keblaam, which shows that its Hebrew had the consonants of the Masoretic Text. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which makes sense as it stands, but the Lucianic reading is attractive and may be original. The Lucianic form is reported from the editions and commentaries and was not checked in a manuscript.

p: Tiphsah is a town on the Euphrates, far from Menahem's reach. The Lucianic Greek has Tappuah, a town near Tirzah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV and most translations
Lucianic Greek manuscripts (Θαφωε), as reported; RSV, NRSV
Codex Vaticanus (as printed by Rahlfs)

why: The only known Tiphsah is Thapsacus on the Euphrates (1 Kings 4:24), hundreds of miles away; Menahem could hardly have attacked it "from Tirzah." Tappuah lay on the border of Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 16:8; Joshua 17:7–8), close to Tirzah, and the two names look alike in Hebrew. Many scholars accept Tappuah. Vaticanus has "Tirzah" here, which makes Menahem attack his own base and looks like a slip from the next words. The Lucianic form is reported from the editions and commentaries and was not checked in a manuscript. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, since an unknown local Tiphsah is possible, but marks the doubt.

p: Kings says Ahaz made "his son" pass through the fire. Chronicles says "his sons."

readings.w: 2 Kings, Masoretic Text
2 Chronicles 28:3 (parallel account)

why: Chronicles generalizes, as it often does when it describes a wicked king, and it also changes "made pass through" to "burned." The Plain translates Kings. Manasseh is later said to have done the same with his son (21:6).

p: The written Hebrew says "Arameans" came to Elath; the reading tradition says "Edomites." The two words differ by one letter.

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); Septuagint ("Idumaeans"); most modern translations
Masoretic written text (Ketiv); KJV ("the Syrians")

why: In Hebrew script d (ד) and r (ר) are easily confused, and "Aram" and "Edom" are mixed up several times in the Bible (2 Samuel 8:12–13). Elath was an Edomite port, Aram never held it long, and Edomites did take back the region in this period (2 Chronicles 28:17). Many scholars think the whole verse first spoke of Edom: "the king of Edom recovered Elath for Edom," with "Rezin" added later, and the RSV and NRSV print the verse that way. The Greek (Vaticanus) keeps "Rezin king of Syria" and "for Syria" but has "Idumaeans" (Edomites) at this word. The Plain follows the reading tradition at this word and keeps "Rezin king of Aram" and "for Aram" as written.

p: The Hebrew names "So king of Egypt." The Greek has "Segor," and the Lucianic text a Nubian "Adrammelech the Ethiopian."

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Latin Vulgate ("Sua"); KJV and most translations
Codex Vaticanus (as printed by Rahlfs)
Lucianic Greek manuscripts, as reported (not checked in a manuscript)
readings.orig: Αδραμελεχ τὸν Αἰθίοπα τὸν κατοικοῦντα ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ
readings.en: Adrammelech the Ethiopian, living in Egypt
readings.plain: Adrammelech the Ethiopian, who lived in Egypt

why: Where "Segor" comes from is unclear. The Lucianic text explains "So" as a king of the Nubian ("Ethiopian") dynasty that was moving into Egypt at the time; its name Adrammelech is perhaps borrowed from 17:31. W. Shea took this as an old clue pointing to the Nubian king Piye. The Plain keeps the Hebrew. On who So was, see the note on this verse.

t: Towns or mountains of the Medes?
p: The Hebrew has "the towns of Media." The Greek has "the mountains of the Medes," one letter different in Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Latin Vulgate ("in civitatibus Medorum"); KJV and most translations
Septuagint (Vaticanus, as printed by Rahlfs)
readings.en: and the mountains of the Medes

why: Hebrew 'are, "towns of," and hare, "mountains of," differ by one letter, and the letters ע and ה were sometimes confused. Media did lie in the Zagros mountains, so the Greek makes sense, but Assyria settled deportees in its new provincial towns there, which fits the Hebrew. The same pair recurs in the parallel at 18:11. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

p: The written Hebrew has "his prophet"; the reading tradition has "the prophets of."

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); KJV ("by all the prophets")
readings.en: by the hand of every prophet of (every seer)

readings.w: Masoretic written text (Ketiv)
readings.en: by the hand of all his prophet(s)

why: The difference is a single letter (y or w), which looked almost the same in later Hebrew script. The reading tradition gives a smoother phrase, "every prophet and every seer," and the Plain follows it. The sense, warnings by many prophets, is the same.

a: Let him go and live there
p: The Hebrew says "let them go and live there," then "let him teach." The Latin makes it all singular; the Greek all plural.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate ("et vadat, et habitet"); most modern translations
readings.en: and let him go and live there
readings.plain: Let him go and live there

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV "let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them"
readings.en: and let them go and live there, and let him teach them
readings.plain: Let them go and live there

readings.w: Septuagint (Vaticanus, as printed by Rahlfs), plural throughout
readings.orig: καὶ πορευέσθωσαν καὶ κατοικείτωσαν ἐκεῖ καὶ φωτιοῦσιν αὐτούς
readings.en: and let them go and live there, and they will teach them
readings.plain: Let them go and live there

why: The order names "one of the priests," and 17:28 says that one priest came, so the singular is smooth and most translations use it. The Hebrew plural may mean the priest went with a party, or it may be a slip. The Greek turns the whole sentence plural. The Plain follows the singular of the Latin here; the Hebrew plural is the harder reading and may be original.
